doc.title: Bernie Kirsh interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 27, 2022

title: Watching Stevie Wonder and the Mahavishnu Orchestra
summary: Before engineering, Kirsh observed Stevie Wonder's synthesizer sessions and then Mahavishnu, which changed his direction. Rowe adds a concert memory.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Am I correct that you recorded Patti Smith’s “Horses” record?
Yeah I did, I did. That was 1975, fall of ’75 I think, October, somewhere in there.
Do you remember what you thought about it at the time? I guess it’s as simple asking did you like it?

I did. I enjoyed her creativity. You know it was, you know just to give you a little background going into that, because this is now five years, four years after I started working at Electric Lady and working as an engineer, I had done a lot of stuff just sitting and watching. The first session I was on observing was Stevie Wonder. I mean this is the kind of stuff that was going on there. And great engineers, Bob Margouleff and Malcolm

Cecil, the two guys that were recording and producing Stevie at the time. And I got to sit and watch these guys and they were developing — they were using Moog synthesizers and they had a one called TONTO was the name, and it was these three huge panels of Moog equipment and so forth, and they would work overnight to create a bass sound or whatever they were doing. So there was that, and then another date comes in and it’s John McLaughlin and the Mahavishnu Orchestra. That’s when my life changed. And I was in the studio setting up, Billy Cobham was the drummer and I was setting up his mics on the drums. And the door opens and John walks in and looking great. I mean up until this point most of what I’d seen were rock groups of the era, that sort of thing. And John came in in a different level of competence and aesthetic. And really all these guys were, they were just great musicians. And I took note of that. I thought you know this is an aesthetic that I really like. This is a high level of communication and competences as players and people were liking it. It was a wide audience and they were trying new things, as were other people coming off the Miles Davis experience at the time, the jazz fusion. And so that kind of locked me in. That was like ’72, ’73 whenever that was.

Yeah, I must insert that I was living in Buffalo at the time and someone gave me tickets to see The Mahavishnu Orchestra, and I didn’t know what or who they were, and wow. I was totally blown away by that.
